quote: But the likelihood of a given state of Nature producing the data we have seen, has nothing to do with the researcher’s private intentions.
content: This is the likelihood principle, and the essay presents it as arithmetic. Whether Bayesian inference is actually immune to optional stopping has since been tested formally, and the answer is: only for a subjective prior that the analyst genuinely holds. de Heide & Grünwald (2021) show that with the default, objective or improper priors that are used in every practical Bayesian analysis, and under any misspecification of the model, a Bayesian who stops on reaching a threshold Bayes factor produces inferences that are wrong in a way that the stopping rule explains; Sanborn & Hills (2014) found that optional stopping inflates Bayes-factor error rates in the regime psychologists actually use, and the reply by Rouder (2014) concedes the point conditional on the prior being true. Jaynes’s two doctors have identical likelihood functions; what they do not have is identical priors, because the second doctor “staked his reputation” on the treatment, and the Bayesian who takes the essay’s advice must condition on that too. The essay is right that the frequentist analysis is awkward and wrong that the Bayesian one is a theorem with no assumptions. The stopping rule enters through the prior, which is not where the essay looked for it.

quote: That’s why we’re interested in Cox’s Theorem and its many extensions, showing that any representation of uncertainty which obeys certain constraints has to map onto probability theory. Coherent math is great, but unique math is even better.
content: Cox’s theorem does not establish uniqueness in the sense the essay needs. Cox’s original argument is incomplete without additional density or continuity assumptions (Halpern (1999) gives a finite counterexample), and Book II’s annotations covered that. The larger problem is the premise: Cox assumes that degrees of plausibility are single real numbers. Every serious rival to probability, imprecise probability (Walley 1991, a book with no DOI), Dempster–Shafer belief functions (Dempster (1967)), possibility theory, rejects exactly that premise, so the theorem does not refute them; it declines to consider them. Dutch-book arguments have the same shape: they establish that credences which are used as fair betting quotients for all bets simultaneously must be probabilities, and the step from “you would lose money if you bet this way” to “your beliefs are irrational” has a literature of objections that the essay treats as nonexistent (Hájek (2005)). Uniqueness given the axioms is a theorem; the axioms are a choice, and the choice is where the dispute with the “toolboxers” actually lives.

quote: But when you can use the exact Bayesian calculation that uses every scrap of available knowledge, you are done. You will never find a statistical method that yields a better answer.
content: This is true when the true data-generating process is inside the model class and false otherwise, and it is never inside the model class. Under misspecification, Bayesian inference can be inconsistent and can be beaten by procedures that are not Bayesian: Grünwald & van Ommen (2017) exhibit a simple linear regression in which standard Bayes converges to a bad model with ever-increasing confidence, and the fix (SafeBayes, tempering the likelihood) is not a Bayesian update from any prior. Diaconis & Freedman (1986) showed inconsistency of Bayes estimates in infinite-dimensional problems even with the truth in the support of the prior. The essay pre-empts these results with a ratchet: any better method must be “using knowledge, perhaps in the form of disguised prior information,” which can be fed back into the Bayesian calculation. But a method that ignores available information (a tempered likelihood, a fast-and-frugal heuristic that discards cues) cannot be re-expressed as a Bayesian calculation that uses every scrap of information, since discarding is what makes it work, and a claim that survives every counterexample by reinterpretation is not a law in the sense the essay wants. The Carnot analogy fails at the same point: Carnot efficiency is a bound that holds for every engine, while Bayes-optimality is a bound that holds only for the engines built inside the model.

quote: You want to use a regularized linear regression, because that works better in practice? Well, that corresponds (says the Bayesian) to having a Gaussian prior over the weights.
content: It corresponds to the mode of the posterior under a Gaussian prior, and the posterior mode is not a Bayesian quantity in any decision-theoretic sense: it is not the Bayes estimator under squared, absolute or any standard loss, it is not invariant under reparametrization of the weights, and a MAP estimate inherits none of the coherence guarantees the essay has just claimed for Bayesian inference. The gap is not academic. Under a Laplace prior the MAP estimate is the lasso and is sparse, while the full posterior under that prior is not sparse at all and contracts at the wrong rate in high dimensions (Castillo, Schmidt-Hieber & van der Vaart (2015)); the method works because the practitioner takes the mode and throws the rest of the posterior away, which is to say because they do not do the Bayesian calculation. “Everything good has a Bayesian interpretation” is true in the trivial sense that any estimator can be written as the argmax of something; the essay needs the strong sense, that the method’s success is explained by the interpretation, and for regularized regression the interpretation predicts the wrong estimator.

quote: Bayesian theorems are elegant, coherent, optimal, and provably unique because they are laws.
content: Two of those adjectives are earned and two are not. Coherent: the probability calculus is consistent relative to set theory, as the essay says. Elegant: granted. Optimal: only under the truth-in-model assumption above, and “optimal” in the decision-theoretic sense requires a loss function the theorems do not supply. Unique: only relative to the Cox or Dutch-book premises, which competitors reject. And the word that does the work, “laws,” imports the essay’s thermodynamic analogy, in which the Second Law constrains every possible engine. Bayesian conditionalization does not have that status even within Bayesian epistemology: the rule that one should update by conditioning is not derivable from the probability axioms and must be argued for separately, by diachronic Dutch books whose force is disputed (Teller (1973) for the argument; Christensen (1991) against), and it is known to be the wrong rule whenever the agent’s evidence is not a proposition learned with certainty (Jeffrey conditioning) or the agent is uncertain about their own credences or about logic. The essay is entitled to prefer the Bayesian framework. It is not entitled to call the preference a law of nature and the alternatives a violation of physics, which is what the next two essays do.
